How we take a website client from a signed quote to a live site, a trained owner and a closed project. Anyone on the team can run the stages. Whoever builds the site also follows the builder appendix at the end.

The whole flow at a glance

Stage Meeting What happens Money
0. Set up none Handoff, folders, Monday board, kickoff invite Deposit paid before anything starts
1. Kickoff 60 min Scope read back, approver named, due dates set, every meeting booked
2. Content and accounts 45-60 min Copy, photos, domain, business email
3. Design direction 45-60 min The look approved on a preview link
4. Halfway review 45 min Design and first pages reviewed. Review gate 1 Invoice 2 once approved in writing
5. Full site review 60 min Every page reviewed. Review gate 2 Final invoice once approved in writing
6. Go live none Client pays hosting, domain connected, site published Only after the final payment clears
7. Training and closeout 60 min Owner trained, handoff, review and referral asks

Landing page only: run stages 2 and 3 as one session.

Timeline: put a timeline in the quote that assumes the client's content will arrive late, and tie it to the copy and photo due dates. If those dates slip, the timeline moves, and you say so in writing.

Who does what

Role Owns Today
Deal owner Whoever closed the deal. The quote, every invoice, payment follow-up, and HubSpot updates within 24 hours. Whoever closed it
Project lead Runs every meeting, books the calendar, sends every recap and weekly update, chases what the client owes, keeps Monday current. Eli
Builder Designs and builds the site, sets up the domain and email with the client, runs the quality checks, publishes. Eli, with Claude

One person can hold all three roles. Write each name on the Monday group at setup.

The rules

  1. No work starts until the quote is signed and the deposit is paid.
  2. The client pays for their own hosting, domain and email mailbox, on their own card and in their own name. BPP never fronts these costs, and never takes a card number by phone, by text or on a call.
  3. One named approver, in writing, before design starts. Ask who else needs to see the work before it's final.
  4. Two review gates. One combined change list at the halfway review (gate 1) and one at the full site review (gate 2). New content or new asks after gate 2 are a change order. Fixing our own mistakes is always free and never counts as a round.
  5. Every approval is in writing. Out loud isn't enough. Send an email and get "approved" back.
  6. The site stays on the staging link until the final payment clears.
  7. Book every remaining meeting before the kickoff call ends.
  8. Ask for an invite, not a password. Webflow, Google Business Profile and HubSpot all let the owner add a person, and many domain companies do too (GoDaddy calls it Delegate Access). If a password truly can't be avoided, it goes in the client's credentials sheet, shared with named people only.
  9. Out-of-scope asks get neither a yes nor a no on the call. Say: "Good idea. That's outside what we scoped, so let me price it and send it over." Never price live. Write it up on the Change Order Form.
  10. Reply to the client within 24 hours. Send a recap the same day as every meeting, and a short status update every week, even when nothing changed.
  11. Someone else on the team clicks through every deliverable before the client sees it.
  12. If an invoice is 7 or more days late, work pauses. That's BPP's standard, and it has to be written into the quote.

What a BPP website includes

Included: a custom Webflow site that works on phones and computers · business email set up (the client pays the mailbox subscription) · a contact form connected to a basic CRM (a free HubSpot account with a simple pipeline), plus training on it · basic on-page SEO.

Not included unless it's on the quote:

  • Writing the copy. The client writes it; we give them prompts and polish it lightly.
  • Logo or brand design.
  • Google Business Profile. It's a separate service, except inside Launch Pad, where it's included.
  • An online store, booking or scheduling, photo proofing galleries, or a blog.
  • Pages beyond the ones listed.
  • Ongoing updates after launch.
  • Hosting, domain and mailbox fees. Those are the client's cost.

Prices and payment splits come from the pricing hub (Service Packages), not from this SOP.

Stage 0: Set up (before kickoff)

Trigger: the quote is signed and the deposit has landed. Check the payment in HubSpot yourself before you book the kickoff.

What every website quote must say (deal owner, before it's sent):

  • Every page by name, and every deliverable on its own line.
  • What "halfway" means. For a full site: design approved, plus the Home page and the next one or two pages built and clickable on the staging link. For a landing page: design approved and the page built on the staging link.
  • The two review gates. New content or new asks after gate 2 are a change order.
  • Response times: the client replies within 2 business days and approves within 5.
  • The final payment clears before the site goes live on their domain.
  • Work pauses if an invoice is 7 or more days late.
  • The client-paid costs, in writing: "Hosting is about $180 a year, the domain about $20 a year, and the email mailbox is billed monthly by Google or Microsoft. All of these are billed to you directly."
  • The payment schedule. Package splits are on the pricing hub. Standalone websites usually pay in three parts: a deposit, the halfway payment, and the final payment before go-live.

Paste-ready wording for these terms is in Website Quote Terms (1. Internal Operations/6. Templates & Resources/1. Proposal & Service Agreeement Templates/website-quote-terms.md). Paste it into the Terms section of the quote.

Steps (project lead, the day the deposit lands):

  1. Fill in the sales-to-delivery handoff (Admin/sales-to-delivery-handoff.md in the client folder): what was sold, anything promised out loud, the real decision-maker, and what success looks like in the client's words. No kickoff until it's filled in.
  2. Set up the client.
    • With Claude: run /bpp-onboard. It builds everything below.
    • By hand:
      • The client folder in SharePoint under 2. Client Operations/, copied from _Client Template.
      • The client's Google Drive folder, with a credentials sheet copied from the Credentials Template.
      • A Monday group made by duplicating "⭐ NEW CLIENT TEMPLATE" on the Client Delivery board.
  3. Edit the access-request email before it goes out so it asks for invites, not logins (rule 8).
  4. On Monday:
    • Rename the four milestone slots: M1 Design direction approved · M2 First pages built · M3 Remaining pages built · M4 Contact form and basic CRM.
    • Add a Business email setup item, and a Go live item between Client Review and Project Close Out.
    • Mark every date provisional until kickoff.
  5. Share the client's Drive folder with the client's email address by name. Never use "anyone with the link."
  6. Send the kickoff invite with a short pre-read: what we'll cover, and what to bring (logo files, three websites they like, their list of services, who approves).

Done when: the deposit is confirmed, the handoff is filled in, the folders and Monday group exist, and the kickoff is booked.

Stage 1: Kickoff (60 minutes)

Goal: leave with the scope confirmed out loud, the approver named, a copy due date, a photo due date, and every remaining meeting on the calendar.

Before you join: confirm the deposit, and have the signed quote and the handoff open.

  1. Open (5 min). "This call has one job: by the end we both know exactly what we're building, what I need from you, and when."
  2. Read the scope back from the quote (10 min). Name every page. Don't make it sound bigger or smaller. Then: "Anything past these pages we handle as a change order, so there are no surprises on either side." Confirm the legal business name for invoices.
  3. Who approves (5 min). "Who makes the final call on the design? Does anyone else need to see it before it's final, like a partner, a board member or family?" Write the name in the recap.
  4. What the site has to do (10 min). Their services. Who they most want to reach and what that visitor should do. Three websites they like and why. Anything they hate.
  5. What we need, with due dates (10 min).
    • Copy: in their words. We send a questionnaire and copy prompts; voice memos are fine.
    • Photos: a set number of web-ready photos per page or category, agreed on the call (up to 12 per category has worked well). They choose them and send one batch through one link by a named date.
    • Logo files: vector (.svg, .ai, .eps) or the largest PNG they have.
    • Testimonials with permission to publish, plus any brand colors or fonts.

  6. Accounts and costs (5 min). Do they own the domain, and where? Who on their side sends the invites? Say the hosting cost out loud:

    "Hosting runs about $180 a year, which works out to $15 a month if you pay yearly. That's billed to your card directly, not through us, and the account is in your name, so you own it outright. The domain is separate and small, usually around $20 a year."

  7. How we work (5 min). They reply within 2 business days and approve within 5. There are two review gates. They tell you their preferred channel (text, call or email) and their best times, and you tell them when each invoice goes out.

  8. Book every meeting (10 min). Put all five remaining sessions on the calendar now, on the same weekday and time if you can. Clients who ignore texts and emails still show up to a calendar invite.

After the call (same day):

  • Recap email: the scope, the approver, every due date, every meeting date, what they owe us, and every out-of-scope ask, including the ones we're doing for free.
  • Monday: replace the provisional dates with the agreed ones.
  • Meeting notes: file them in the client's Admin/Meetings/ folder. With Claude, use bpp-meeting-sync. By hand, write five lines: decisions, dates, what they owe, what we owe, out-of-scope asks.
  • HubSpot: log the call.

Done when: the recap is sent and every meeting is booked.

Stage 2: Content and accounts (45-60 minutes)

Goal: everything the build depends on is in hand or has a date. The builder joins this session.

  1. Copy. Go through the questionnaire together if it isn't filled in. Capture answers live.
  2. Domain.
    • If they have one: confirm who owns it, which company it's registered with, and that they can log in. The builder checks it's active (appendix).
    • If they don't: they buy it on the call, in their own account. It costs around $20 a year.
  3. Old accounts. Ask about any old website or email service that ever used the domain (Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy email and so on). An old email account can block the new one.
  4. Business email. The builder sets it up live with the client, in the client's own Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 account, bought directly from Google or Microsoft. The client enters their own card. Send and receive a test.
  5. Invites. The client adds us as a user wherever we need access.
  6. Photos. The client shares the folder with us by name. Open a few files on the call to prove we can download them.

Design (stage 3) doesn't wait on email. The contact form and go-live do.

After: send a recap of what's in, what's still owed, and the dates.

Done when:

  • Copy and photos are received, or have dates.
  • The domain is active and in the client's name.
  • Email sends and receives, or there's a written plan and date to fix whatever is blocking it.

Stage 3: Design direction (45-60 minutes)

Goal: the approver signs off on the look before the full build.

  1. The builder shows the homepage direction on a link: colors, fonts, photo style and layout. Placeholder copy is fine. Show one direction, two at most.
  2. Recommend first, then ask: "Here's what I'd go with and why. How does this feel to you?"
  3. Write down every reaction.

After: send a written summary of the agreed direction (palette, fonts, homepage layout) and ask for "approved."

Done when: the named approver has approved the direction in writing. If the approver wasn't on the call, it isn't approved yet.

Between meetings: the build

The builder:

  • Builds on the staging link (the free clientname.webflow.io preview). No hosting plan and no custom domain until go-live.
  • Works page by page: Home first, then the halfway pages, then the rest.
  • Runs the quality checks in the appendix before any client sees a link.
  • Moves each Monday status the same day the work changes.

The project lead:

  • Sends the weekly status update.
  • Tracks what the client owes. If a blocking item is 2 or more business days late, tell the client in writing that day, with the effect on the timeline. Don't absorb a slip silently.

Stage 4: Halfway review (45 minutes)

Goal: the design and first pages are reviewed and the gate 1 changes are agreed.

  1. Walk the staging link on screen, then show it on a phone.
  2. Collect every change into one list. This is review gate 1. Read the list back before you hang up.
  3. Tell them what happens next: "I'll send the list and an approval request tonight. Once you reply 'approved,' invoice two goes out."

After:

  • Send a recap the same day with the gate 1 list and a request for written approval of the design and the halfway pages.
  • When "approved" comes back, the deal owner sends invoice 2 from HubSpot, on the deal. Each payment gets one invoice in one system, so check QuickBooks isn't already billing it.
  • Move Halfway to Done on Monday.

Done when: the written approval is in, invoice 2 is sent, and the change list is agreed.

Stage 5: Full site review (60 minutes)

Before the call:

  • Every page is built and the gate 1 changes are done.
  • Someone else on the team has clicked through the whole site.
  • A test submission of the contact form has landed in the client's inbox and in their basic CRM.
  1. Walk every page on a computer and on a phone.
  2. Collect one combined final list. This is review gate 2. Say it plainly: "This is the last round. Anything new after this, we'll price separately."
  3. Show how leads will reach them: the form, their inbox and their basic CRM.

After:

  • Make the gate 2 changes, then send a "ready for final approval" email with the staging link.
  • When "approved" comes back, the deal owner sends the final invoice.
  • If there's no reply within 5 business days, follow up in writing that day.

Done when: the written final approval is in and the final invoice is sent.

Stage 6: Go live (after the final payment clears)

  1. The deal owner confirms the final payment has cleared.
  2. The builder sends the Webflow hosting payment request to the client's email (see the Webflow Client Hosting SOP). The client accepts and adds their own card.
  3. The builder connects the domain, publishes and runs the live checks (appendix).
  4. The client gets a content editor seat so they can edit text and photos.
  5. Swap any staging links we've shared (for example, BPP's "Sites we built" showcase) to the live address.
  6. Tell the client it's live, and send the link.

If the final payment doesn't come, the site stays on the staging link and the deal owner follows up.

Done when: the site loads on the client's domain, the form works there, and the client has their editor seat.

Stage 7: Training and closeout (60 minutes)

  1. Walk the live site together.
  2. Train them on editing text and photos, and on how leads arrive (their inbox and their basic CRM). Record a short walkthrough video (Loom) of each, and leave the written quick-start guides in their Drive folder under Training Documents/.
  3. Hand over a list of every account they own (domain, hosting, email, basic CRM) and who to call for what.
  4. Make the asks, in this order:
    • How did we do? (the survey)
    • A Google review
    • A testimonial (offer to use the good things they said during the project, in their own words)
    • Permission to show their site in BPP's showcase
    • A referral (terms in the Partner Referral SOP)
    • The next phase of work, if there is one

After:

  • Close the Monday items, and mark the HubSpot deal won with notes.
  • Add the client's entry to the client Lessons Learned log, and write the final client-memory.md entry.

Done when: the client is trained, the asks are made, Monday and HubSpot are closed, and the lesson is logged.

When things go sideways

What happens What to do
The client goes quiet After 2 business days on a blocking item, write to them that day with the effect on the timeline. Use the channel they prefer. If they prefer text and there's no reply in 3-5 hours, text again.
The client asks to pause Confirm the pause in writing: what's been delivered, what's been paid, and what's owed when work restarts. Agree how it restarts: they reach out, or on a check-in date they pick. Clear the Monday dates with a note, keep personal reasons out of shared tools, and don't chase.
An invoice is 7+ days late Work pauses (rule 12). The deal owner follows up.
A new decision-maker shows up late Changes to work that's already approved are a paid extension, not free rework.
An out-of-scope ask Sort it into one of three buckets. Gift: under 30 minutes and nothing to maintain (social icons, an embed); call it a gift. Their tool: something a paid service already does (booking, proofing galleries, print sales); they own the subscription and we link to it. Change order: real hours or ongoing upkeep (extra pages, copywriting, SEO work, logo, store). Reframe before you price: five gallery pages is usually one gallery with filters.
The domain or email won't verify The builder checks the domain's status and any old email account first (appendix), before touching any settings. Only the owner can get the domain company to fix a hold, so the client makes that call.
The client wants to "own" the site They already own the hosting and the domain. To edit the site themselves, they need a content editor seat. A full transfer is rare (Webflow Client Hosting SOP).

Words you'll hear

  • Staging link: the free preview address (clientname.webflow.io) where we build and review. It isn't the real site.
  • Hosting (site plan): the yearly Webflow fee that keeps the site live on the client's own address. About $180 a year, paid by the client.
  • Domain: the address, like theirbusiness.com, bought from a domain company (GoDaddy, Squarespace and others) for about $20 a year. The client owns it.
  • DNS: the settings at the domain company that point the domain at the website and the email.
  • Basic CRM: a free HubSpot account where contact-form leads land, with a simple pipeline (new lead, contacted, won or lost).
  • Review gate: a point where the client approves in writing before we move on. There are two.
  • Change order: a written, priced add-on the client signs before we do the extra work.

Builder appendix (Eli, Claude, future builders)

Setup

  • Create the client's site by hand in BPP's Webflow workspace (the Webflow API can't create a site). Stay on the free staging plan.
  • Build locally first under build-loop, with one folder per client: a spec (pages and acceptance checks), design tokens, a change list per round, and a release record for every publish.

Quality checks before any client sees a link

  • Check every page at 1440, 820, 390 and 320 pixels wide. Nothing should scroll sideways.
  • Look at it on a real phone. Automated checks can pass while the page still looks wrong on a phone.
  • Text contrast passes WCAG AA.
  • Every link and button works, including the phone menu.
  • No invented copy. Every sentence traces back to the client's words or is clearly marked as a placeholder.
  • design-qa-gate returns SHIP.
  • Publish only when the project lead says go.

Domain and business email (stage 2)

  • Domain status: for a .com or .net, run whois -h whois.verisign-grs.com "domain example.com" | grep -iE "status|updated".
    • clientHold or serverHold means the domain is frozen at the registry. No DNS change can fix that.
    • Only the owner can get the domain company to lift the hold. Have them name the status code and ask for the domains team.
    • The "Updated Date" tells you whether anything actually changed, whatever support says.
  • Old email accounts: if the domain was ever on Google Workspace, even one resold through Wix or GoDaddy, that old account still holds the domain after it lapses. Google won't verify the domain for a new account until the owner either recovers the old one (admin.google.com) or releases the domain (Google's "domain already in use" form).
    • Removing the domain from a reseller account can take 7 days before it can be added again.
    • Don't start a second sign-up while you're checking: a half-finished sign-up holds the domain too.
  • Setup:
    • Buy Google Workspace Business Starter (or Microsoft 365) directly, on the client's card.
    • Verify the domain with the TXT record at the domain company, then add the MX records.
    • Send and receive a test.
  • No domain yet: the client buys it in their own account on the call. Never buy it for them.

Contact form and basic CRM

  • Create a free HubSpot account in the client's name, with their business email as the login. Add a simple deal pipeline.
  • Send form notifications to their business email, and add an email filter so leads never land in spam.
  • Submit one real test from a phone (bot protection blocks automated tests). Confirm it reaches their inbox and the basic CRM, then delete the test records.
  • Leave them a one-page quick-start guide (PDF).

Launch checklist (stage 6)

  1. The deal owner confirms the final payment cleared.
  2. Send the hosting payment request: Webflow dashboard → Client management → Clients → Send a payment request. Choose the client's site, the Basic plan, yearly, to the client's email.
  3. Once the plan is active, connect the domain in Webflow (root and www).
  4. At the domain company, replace the old website's records with Webflow's. Keep the email (MX) records.
  5. Publish.
  6. Live checks:
    • Root and www both load over https.
    • Every page loads.
    • The form submits on the live domain.
    • Page titles, descriptions and the social share image are set.
    • The staging address isn't indexed by search engines.
  7. Give the client a content editor seat on their site only. Check seat availability on the invite screen before promising it.
  8. If the client has a Google Business Profile, update its website field.
  9. Swap BPP's showcase link from the staging link to the live address, and republish.

Webflow traps we've hit

  • When you re-send a page's custom code, include its script tags, or the scripts quietly disappear.
  • Generated inline classes can collide across pages. Use named classes.
  • Publishing twice within about a minute hits a rate limit. Wait a minute.
  • Uploaded variable fonts lose their width range. Keep your own @font-face with the range in the page code.
